Ugh, that’s really frustrating. When you’re putting in effort and the scale just sits there, it can feel defeating.

A few really common things can make this happen even when someone is trying hard:

• Calories sneaking in (sauces, drinks, snacks, portion sizes)  
• Eating very little during the week but more on weekends  
• Water retention from stress, sleep, hormones, or new exercise  
• Gaining a bit of muscle while losing fat (the scale stays similar)  
• Tracking methods being a bit off (this happens to almost everyone)

A couple questions that might help figure it out:

• What kinds of things have you been doing to try to lose weight? (diet changes, calorie tracking, exercise, etc.)  
• Has your weight stayed exactly the same, or has it fluctuated up and down?  
• Have measurements, clothes fit, or photos changed at all?

We can troubleshoot it together. Plateaus are super common and usually fixable once you find the thing that’s blocking progress.

It’s really normal to feel that way the day before surgery. A lot of people have the same “what if I don’t wake up?” thought when they hear they’ll be under anesthesia. The reassuring part is that modern anesthesia is very safe, and the entire anesthesia team’s job is to watch you continuously while you’re asleep—your breathing, heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure, and more. Feeling nervous doesn’t mean something bad is going to happen—it just means you’re facing something important and unfamiliar.

A few things that sometimes help tonight:
- Talk with the anesthesiologist or surgeon tomorrow and tell them you’re anxious. They’re used to this and can walk you through exactly what will happen.
- Focus on the next small step rather than the whole surgery.
- Try slow breathing: inhale for 4 seconds, exhale for 6 seconds for a few minutes.

Breakups can leave a really deep imprint, especially when the relationship mattered a lot. Two years might feel like “it should be over by now,” but there isn’t a fixed timeline for grief. For some people, the loss of a relationship hits a lot like any other major loss, and it can take a long time for the feelings to loosen their grip.

The thought “I’ll never find love again” is also a really common one after a painful breakup. When you’ve been hurt deeply, your brain tries to protect you by assuming the worst or by making the future feel closed off. That feeling can be very convincing, but it isn’t a reliable prediction about your life.

What matters more is how stuck or heavy things still feel for you now. If the hurt is still intense after two years, it might really help to talk it through with someone supportive—like a therapist, counselor, or even a support group. A good therapist can help you process what happened and slowly rebuild a sense that your future relationships are possible and safe again.

In the meantime, a few gentle things that sometimes help people in your situation:
- letting yourself grieve the relationship without judging the timeline  
- reconnecting with parts of life that are yours alone (friends, interests, routines)  
- noticing when your mind jumps to absolute conclusions about the future and gently questioning them

And just to say: many people who once felt exactly like you do now eventually do love again—even if it didn’t feel imaginable at the time.

If you’re comfortable sharing, what part of the breakup still hurts the most these days?

The saloon had gone quiet enough to hear the lantern glass ticking in the heat.

Two men stood facing each other across a scarred poker table. Between them sat a leather bag heavy enough to sag the wood beneath it. Gold had a way of pulling silence out of a room.

Caleb Rourke’s hand hovered near his revolver, fingers loose, patient. Dust still clung to his coat from the trail.

Across from him, Mason Pike leaned with one hip against the bar rail, hat tipped low. His eyes never left the bag.

“You always did get greedy,” Mason said softly.

Caleb nudged the bag with two fingers. Coins clinked inside, a bright, treacherous sound. “Funny thing about gold. Makes men remember what’s theirs.”

“Nothing in that bag’s yours.”

A chair creaked somewhere behind them. Nobody moved.

Caleb’s hand drifted lower toward his holster.

Mason’s didn’t.

Instead, there was the faint scrape of steel.

A knife slid into Mason’s hand, thin and mean-looking, catching the lamplight. Fast as a striking snake.

Caleb’s eyes flicked down—just once.

That was enough.

Mason lunged across the table, knife flashing. Caleb shoved the table forward hard, the legs screeching across the floor. The bag of gold toppled, spilling coins that rang across the boards like tiny bells.

The knife slashed past Caleb’s chest, close enough to slice his coat. Caleb grabbed Mason’s wrist with both hands and drove him sideways into the bar. Bottles rattled violently.

They crashed to the floor in a tangle of boots and elbows.

Mason still had the knife.

Caleb slammed his forearm into Mason’s throat, forcing his arm back, but Mason twisted and drove the blade forward. Caleb jerked away—too slow. The knife punched into the meat of his side.

Caleb sucked in a sharp breath. The shock of it froze him for half a heartbeat.

Mason grinned through his teeth. “Got you.”

Caleb answered by smashing his forehead straight into Mason’s nose.

The crack echoed through the saloon.

Mason’s grip faltered. Caleb wrenched the knife hand aside and hammered Mason’s wrist against the floor until the blade clattered away.

They rolled apart, both scrambling.

Coins shifted under Caleb’s boots as he staggered up, one hand clamped tight against his side. Dark wetness spread through his fingers.

Across the room Mason wiped blood from under his nose, eyes burning.

Both men reached for their guns.

The saloon held its breath.

The precinct after midnight had the kind of lighting that made every face look guilty. One buzzing bulb overhead. One dead fly on the windowsill. The room smelled like stale coffee, cheap tobacco, and the slow rot of bad decisions.

I sat in a metal chair that had seen more confessions than a church pew.

Detective Harlan stood behind me, flipping through a thick city phone book like he was looking up a pizza joint. Detective Ruiz leaned against the desk, cigarette dangling from his lip, ash hanging on for dear life.

Ruiz squinted at me through the smoke. “You know why you’re here, Marlowe?”

I tasted blood where I’d bitten my cheek earlier. Copper and regret.

“Parking violation?” I said.

The phone book came down on my ribs with a heavy thud. Not loud. Not sharp. Just deep.

Like getting punched by a dictionary.

Air slipped out of my lungs and didn’t hurry back.

“Cute,” Harlan said from behind me. “He thinks he’s cute.”

My side burned. The kind of pain that spreads slow, like whiskey on an empty stomach. No marks tomorrow. That was the idea. Phone books were the gentleman’s way to break a man.

Ruiz flicked ash on the floor and crouched in front of me.

“You were at the Rialto last night,” he said. “Guy named Benny Costa ends up floating in the river this morning. Funny timing.”

“Lots of people go to the Rialto,” I said.

The phone book hit my shoulder this time.

Thump.

My teeth clicked together.

The room smelled stronger now. Cheap tobacco and sweat. Ruiz’s cigarette was the discount kind that smelled like burned rope and bad life choices.

I breathed through my nose. Big mistake. The smoke crawled in and sat there.

“You private dicks always think you’re smarter than cops,” Ruiz said. “That the badge makes us stupid.”

Another thud. Lower back.

Pain spread out like a dark stain.

I counted the seconds. Old trick. Pain behaves better if you give it numbers.

One. Two. Three.

“You’re making this harder than it needs to be,” Harlan said.

“Story of my life,” I muttered.

The book came down again.

For a moment the room tilted sideways. The fly on the windowsill looked like it was swimming.

Ruiz sighed and stood up, pacing slow.

“You know what I hate?” he said. “Heroes. Guys who think they’re gonna hold the line.”

I laughed. It came out crooked.

“Buddy,” I said, wincing as my ribs reminded me they existed, “if I was a hero… I wouldn’t be working divorce cases for sixty bucks a day.”

Harlan leaned close behind my ear. I could smell his aftershave fighting a losing war with bourbon.

“Then tell us about Benny Costa.”

I looked at the flickering light. Thought about the river. Thought about the girl who’d hired me.

And mostly I thought about that phone book.

“Sure,” I said.

Ruiz raised an eyebrow.

I took a slow breath through the smoke and pain.

“Soon as you boys finish reading it to me.”
:::

The news anchor’s voice was low and practiced, the cadence of tragedy packaged for broadcast. On the screen, a photograph of the target hovered beside a scrolling caption.

“Business magnate…”

The man in the hotel chair didn’t look up immediately. He turned the rifle under the lamplight with the same quiet patience a watchmaker might give a movement. The metal carried a faint, cold sheen. His fingers rested along the receiver, steady, unhurried.

The job had a number. The number had a fee. The fee had cleared.

Everything else was administrative noise.

He rotated the bolt between his fingers, examining the lugs and the extractor. Carbon residue traced faint shadows along the steel. He wiped it away with slow, economical movements. No hurry. No hesitation. Just maintenance of equipment.

On television, the anchor continued.

“Authorities say the businessman had recently—”

He muted the sound.

The silence improved concentration.

He tilted the rifle slightly, peering through the chamber end toward the barrel, inspecting the clean geometry of rifling spiraling away into darkness. Precision engineering. Reliable tools deserved attention; neglected tools created variables. Variables complicated contracts.

His cloth passed along the barrel exterior, then over the muzzle crown, careful not to nick the symmetry there. Even microscopic deformities could alter trajectory. Physics did not forgive carelessness.

People did.

People invented motives, emotions, redemption stories. They wrapped death in philosophy.

He preferred the language of tolerances and mechanisms.

The optic sat mounted above the receiver, glass reflecting the muted hotel lamp. He adjusted one turret a fraction, then returned it. Not correction—confirmation. The clicks were crisp, measured. Predictable.

Predictability was the entire profession.

On the television screen, footage rolled: the target exiting a black sedan days earlier, smiling for cameras, surrounded by microphones and security.

The man in the chair watched for a moment.

Not with anger. Not with interest.

Assessment.

Height. Posture. The habitual tilt of the head when answering questions. Small details that belonged in the same mental category as wind drift or mechanical zero. Data points.

He set the bolt back beside the rifle and wiped his hands with a clean cloth.

People liked to imagine killers as creatures of emotion—rage, revenge, bloodlust. It helped them understand something they otherwise could not accept.

But this was not personal.

It was clerical.

A contract was an agreement between parties. One side required an outcome. The other side possessed the capability to produce it. Money bridged the distance between those two facts.

Life and death were not the point.

The basement door groaned when Lena pushed it open, the sound dragging through the quiet house like something waking up.

Cold air drifted up the stairs. Damp. Sour. The kind of smell that made her throat tighten before she even understood why.

“Hello?” she called softly.

No answer. Just the slow drip of something hitting concrete somewhere in the dark.

She descended one step at a time, the wooden stairs creaking under her weight. Her phone flashlight trembled in her hand, the beam bouncing across stacked boxes, old shelves, a rusted washer.

Then the light caught a shoe.

A white sneaker she recognized immediately.

“Jess?”

The beam moved higher.

Jess was slumped against a support post, head tilted at a wrong angle, hair hanging forward like a curtain. Her arms were bound behind the beam with thick tape, the silver surface catching the light in dull flashes.

Lena’s breath left her in a thin whimper.

“No. No, no…”

She stumbled forward, the beam shaking wildly now. The smell was stronger here—metallic and stale, like old pennies and wet wood.

“Jess, wake up,” she whispered, even though something deep in her chest already knew.

Her light slipped past Jess and landed on the far wall.

Lena froze.

More shapes.

At first they looked like piles of laundry slumped along the concrete. Then the light steadied and the shapes became people.

Mark lay near the furnace, motionless, one arm stretched out as if he’d tried to crawl. Tyler sat propped against the wall, chin dropped to his chest, dark stains soaking the front of his flannel. Someone had wrapped string lights around the pipes above him, the bulbs glowing faintly red like a sick joke of Christmas decorations.

And in the center of the room—

Lena’s stomach twisted.

A chair.

Someone was tied to it.

The figure stirred weakly when the light hit their face.

“Lena…?”

It was Kara.

Alive.

Lena gasped and rushed forward, nearly slipping on the damp floor.

“I’m here,” she said, voice shaking. “I’m here.”

Kara’s eyes widened, not with relief—but with terror.

“Lena,” she whispered urgently. “You have to run.”

Behind Lena, at the top of the basement stairs, the door slowly creaked shut.

The prison had no bars.

From the outside, the Halcyon Rehabilitation Complex looked like a research campus—white glass, low buildings, wind combing through silver grass. Visitors expected razor wire and towers. Instead there were quiet corridors and doors that opened with a whisper.

Inside each room sat a chair.

The chair was where the sentence happened.

They called the process Restorative Immersion. Judges preferred the phrase “empathetic correction.” The inmates had simpler names for it: drowning, haunting, the Loop.

Elias Ward was brought to Chamber 12 on his first day.

“Sit,” said the technician.

He sat.

Thin cables unfolded from the chair like metal vines and settled against his temples. The screen in front of him showed a still image: a grocery store parking lot under yellow evening light. The picture looked ordinary. Quiet.

Elias recognized it instantly.

“Wait,” he said.

“Immersion beginning,” the technician replied.

The world vanished.

Then he was somewhere else.

Not watching.

Living.

His hands were smaller. There were grocery bags biting into his fingers. A car key pressed between his knuckles. The air smelled like hot asphalt and detergent from the laundromat next door.

Confusion flickered first.

A strange sense that something was wrong, that the body he inhabited wasn’t his. But the memory didn’t allow distance. Thoughts slid into place that weren’t Elias’s.

Did I remember the milk?

Where are my glasses?

Is someone behind me?

Then footsteps.

Elias felt the moment the victim felt them—before turning, before understanding. A subtle tightening in the chest. Instinct whispering that the world had shifted half a degree toward danger.

He tried to look away.

The memory would not let him.

He turned.

A figure approached quickly from between the parked cars. Face hidden under a hood. Something metallic in his hand.

Elias knew the face under that hood.

His own.

The victim’s mind didn’t recognize it. To them it was just a stranger moving too fast.

“Hey—”

The first spike of fear hit like ice water in the lungs. Not a scream yet. Not panic. Just the sudden collapse of normal life.

This shouldn’t be happening.

The grocery bags slipped from their fingers. Or his fingers. Apples rolled across the pavement.

“Take it,” the victim said quickly. “Just take—”

The words shook. Elias felt their voice tremble from the inside.

The terror grew not as a burst but as a crushing pressure. The realization that this moment might not end. That the stranger’s eyes held something cold and decided.

Time slowed.

The victim’s heart hammered so hard it hurt. Every sound sharpened: wind scraping a cart across concrete, distant traffic, breath turning ragged.

Please let this stop.

The thought came with a desperate bargaining instinct. Wallet. Phone. Anything. The human mind clawing for a path back to normal life.

Elias wanted to scream that it would be okay.

But he knew the truth.

He had written the ending.

When the weapon lifted, the victim’s fear became absolute. Not cinematic. Not dramatic.

Small.

Fragile.

A collapsing understanding: I am going to die here in a parking lot while the sun is still out.

The terror was not loud.

It was heavy.

It pressed on the lungs, thick as gravity. The victim’s mind raced through flashes—faces, unfinished plans, the absurd thought about the milk still sitting in the trunk.

Then the final moment arrived.

Not pain first.

Shock.

Confusion.

The body folding.

The sky tilting.

The terrible, helpless awareness of life slipping sideways out of reach.

And underneath it all: the vast, suffocating fear of disappearing.

Elias felt every second of it.

When the memory ended, he was back in the chair.

He vomited onto the floor.

The technician watched calmly, recording neural data.

“That,” she said softly, “was minute one.”

Elias lifted his head, shaking.

“How many minutes were there?” he whispered.

She checked the tablet.

“According to the victim’s neural reconstruction,” she said, “four hundred and twelve seconds.”

She paused.

“Your sentence requires you to experience them all.”

The cables tightened slightly against his temples as the system prepared the next immersion.

Outside, the campus lawns moved gently in the wind, quiet as ever.

Inside Chamber 12, the parking lot waited.

His hands were smaller. There were grocery bags biting into his fingers. A car key pressed between his knuckles. The air smelled like hot asphalt and detergent from the laundromat next door.

Confusion flickered first.

A strange sense that something was wrong, that the body he inhabited wasn’t his. But the memory didn’t allow distance. Thoughts slid into place that weren’t Elias’s.

Did I remember the milk?

Where are my glasses?

Is someone behind me?

Then footsteps.

Elias felt the moment the victim felt them—before turning, before understanding. A subtle tightening in the chest. Instinct whispering that the world had shifted half a degree toward danger.

He tried to look away.

The memory would not let him.

He turned.

A figure approached quickly from between the parked cars. Face hidden under a hood. Something metallic in his hand.

Elias knew the face under that hood.

His own.

The victim’s mind didn’t recognize it. To them it was just a stranger moving too fast.

“Hey—”

The first spike of fear hit like ice water in the lungs. Not a scream yet. Not panic. Just the sudden collapse of normal life.

This shouldn’t be happening.

The grocery bags slipped from their fingers. Or his fingers. Apples rolled across the pavement.

“Take it,” the victim said quickly. “Just take—”

The words shook. Elias felt their voice tremble from the inside.

The terror grew not as a burst but as a crushing pressure. The realization that this moment might not end. That the stranger’s eyes held something cold and decided.

Time slowed.

The victim’s heart hammered so hard it hurt. Every sound sharpened: wind scraping a cart across concrete, distant traffic, breath turning ragged.

Please let this stop.

The thought came with a desperate bargaining instinct. Wallet. Phone. Anything. The human mind clawing for a path back to normal life.

Elias wanted to scream that it would be okay.

But he knew the truth.

He had written the ending.

When the weapon lifted, the victim’s fear became absolute. Not cinematic. Not dramatic.

Small.

Fragile.

A collapsing understanding: I am going to die here in a parking lot while the sun is still out.

The terror was not loud.

It was heavy.

It pressed on the lungs, thick as gravity. The victim’s mind raced through flashes—faces, unfinished plans, the absurd thought about the milk still sitting in the trunk.

Then the final moment arrived.

Not pain first.

Shock.

Confusion.

The body folding.

The sky tilting.

The terrible, helpless awareness of life slipping sideways out of reach.

And underneath it all: the vast, suffocating fear of disappearing.

Elias felt every second of it.

When the memory ended, he was back in the chair.

He vomited onto the floor.

The technician watched calmly, recording neural data.

“That,” she said softly, “was minute one.”

Elias lifted his head, shaking.

“How many minutes were there?” he whispered.

She checked the tablet.

“According to the victim’s neural reconstruction,” she said, “four hundred and twelve seconds.”

She paused.

“Your sentence requires you to experience them all.”

The cables tightened slightly against his temples as the system prepared the next immersion.

Outside, the campus lawns moved gently in the wind, quiet as ever.

Inside Chamber 12, the parking lot waited.

Somewhere behind them, their child sobs their name.

The tip of the blade stops a breath away.

And in that suspended second, despair settles in their chest like a stone—heavy, inevitable, already falling.

“Careful with that corner,” Sal said, scrubbing in tight circles. “Blood gets into the grout, it’s a whole personality.”

Marta glanced over. “You say that like you’re surprised. Grout is basically a sponge with a bad attitude.”

Sal leaned back on his heels. “Still better than that fish market job.”

Marta groaned immediately. “Don’t. I just got the smell of that out of my brain.”

“Guy goes down face-first into a tuna display,” Sal continued anyway. “Blood, fish guts, melted ice. Looked like a seafood smoothie.”

“Stop talking.”

“I’m just saying, this?” He gestured at the reddish water in the bucket. “This is practically housekeeping.”

Marta dipped her mop again. “Housekeeping doesn’t usually involve bullet holes in the drywall.”

“Bullet holes are easy. Spackle, paint, done. You remember the carpeted staircase in Queens?”

She froze mid-swipe. “The one with the dog?”

“The *three* dogs.”

Marta shut her eyes. “I had to throw out my boots.”

“You loved those boots.”

“They were suede, Sal. Suede!” She scrubbed harder. “And the smell wouldn’t leave. I tried vinegar, baking soda, that industrial enzyme stuff—”

“Yeah, but the boss tipped well.”

“For emotional damages,” she muttered.

Sal stood, stretching his back. “You know what the worst part of this line of work is?”

“The blood?”

“No.”

“The bodies?”

“Nope.”

Marta sighed. “What then?”

Sal nodded toward the hallway. “White tile. Whoever designs places with white tile clearly never planned on anything interesting happening.”

Marta looked at the floor they’d been scrubbing for the past hour and sighed. “Next time we tell them: darker colors. Burgundy. Really hides the memories.”

Sal chuckled, rinsing the rag. “Burgundy. Classy. Matches the clientele, too.”

The first shove barely registered—just another ripple in the crowd.

Then the ground seemed to tilt.

Someone slammed into his back. Another shoulder crushed into his chest. The noise changed from chatter to a roar of panicked voices and pounding feet. The crowd stopped behaving like people and became something else—one massive, surging weight.

He tried to step sideways. There was nowhere to go.

Bodies pressed in from every direction. His arms were pinned to his sides. The air vanished, squeezed out of his lungs by the crush around him. Every breath came thinner than the last, like trying to inhale through cloth.

"Stop!" someone screamed.

But the crowd had no ears.

He focused on one thing—air. Just one full breath. He lifted his chin, trying to find a pocket of space above the shoulders around him. The sky flickered into view between moving heads.

He dragged in half a breath.

Behind him the crowd surged again, and the ground rolled with it, swallowing voices, footsteps, and anything that fell too low to rise again.

The alley behind the embassy was a dead end.

He knew it the moment the second pair of boots rounded the corner. One ahead, two behind. No gaps. No shadows left to disappear into.

The radio in his ear crackled once, then died.

So this was it.

He leaned against the damp brick wall as if catching his breath, fingers slipping calmly into the lining of his coat. The tiny capsule rested exactly where it had for the past three years—smooth, glassy, absurdly small for something that had always felt so heavy.

Footsteps approached, cautious now.

“Hands where we can see them!”

He rolled the pill between thumb and forefinger for a moment. Funny. After all the briefings, all the warnings, he had imagined this moment would feel dramatic. Heroic, even.

Instead it felt quiet.

Almost administrative.

He slipped it into his mouth and bit down.

The capsule cracked with a faint, brittle pop.

At first there was only a sharp bitterness flooding his tongue, chemical and metallic. Then the heat came—sudden and wrong—spreading down his throat and into his chest as if he'd swallowed fire that refused to burn out.

His lungs seized.

Air went in, but it didn’t seem to do anything. The world tilted slightly. The brick wall against his back felt colder, distant, like it belonged to someone else.

Boots rushed toward him now.

“Stop! Don’t—”

Too late.

A violent tremor ran through his muscles. His heart slammed once, twice, wildly out of rhythm. The alley sharpened with strange clarity—the yellow streetlight, the damp smell of rain, a scrap of newspaper dragging along the ground.

So this is how it ends, he thought.

Not with answers. Not with rescue. Just a narrowing tunnel of sound and light.

The cold realization arrived with surprising calm: there would be no interrogation room, no broken secrets, no long prison years.

Only this.

His fingers slackened at his sides. The shouting voices around him sounded very far away now.

For a brief second he felt oddly relieved.

Then the light at the end of the alley dimmed, and the world folded quietly into black.
:::

The road is suddenly quiet.

A few seconds earlier it held the scream of an engine and the rising whine of speed. Now there’s only the faint ticking of hot metal cooling somewhere in the weeds. The motorcycle lies thirty yards back, half on its side, front wheel slowly turning, fairings shattered into black and red fragments scattered across the asphalt like dropped tools.

A glove rests in the middle of the lane. A mirror farther away. Small pieces of plastic glitter in the sunlight.

The rider is motionless near the shoulder where the slide finally stopped. One leg lies at an angle legs aren’t meant to hold, twisted slightly outward beneath torn riding pants. The other is stretched stiff, boot scraped and scuffed pale against the pavement. His jacket is shredded along one side where the asphalt ground through it; the fabric is frayed and dark with dust and grit.

The road rash shows where the gear failed—long, raw scrapes along his forearm and shoulder, skin abraded by the slide, packed with gray road dust. It looks less like a clean wound and more like something sanded away.

A helmet lies a few feet from him, visor cracked, slowly rocking until it settles.

Nothing moves now except a loose scrap of plastic tapping lightly against the pavement in the breeze, and somewhere in the distance, the faint sound of a car that hasn’t yet reached the curve.

:::writing
I heard it before I saw it.

Branches clicked together somewhere behind me, too heavy for the wind. I kept walking down the narrow trail, pretending the forest sounded normal. Pretending the slow crunch of leaves behind my steps wasn’t matching my pace.

Crunch.  
Step.  
Crunch.

When I finally turned, the trees were empty.

For a moment I almost laughed at myself.

Then something moved between the trunks.

It stepped into the thin wash of moonlight—just a man at first, hunched forward, breathing hard like he’d been running. His shirt clung to his back with sweat. His head hung low, hair hiding his face.

“Hey,” I called, my voice smaller than I meant it to be.

He didn’t answer.

His shoulders jerked.

At first I thought he was coughing. Then I heard it—the sound like thick branches snapping under snow.

Crack.

The man folded in on himself with a choking gasp. His spine arched so violently I heard the joints pop down his back one by one. He tried to stand straight again but his body refused, bending wrong, bending forward.

Another crack.

His arm snapped outward at the elbow, stretching longer than it should. He screamed then, a wet, animal sound, while the bones beneath his skin forced new shapes. The sleeves of his shirt tightened as his forearms lengthened, muscles knotting and swelling beneath the fabric.

I couldn’t move.

His fingers spread against the dirt. They kept spreading, joints pushing farther apart until the knuckles bulged. Nails darkened, thickened, curving slowly into black claws that gouged the soil.

The skin along his back pulled tight.

I saw it ripple.

Something underneath was growing, pushing outward. The spine rose in sharp ridges beneath the skin before it tore through the cloth of his shirt. Not blood—just the horrible stretching of flesh as coarse gray hair burst through like frost across glass.

He tried to breathe through it, dragging air in ragged bursts.

Crack. Crack. Crack.

His legs broke next.

They bent backward with a sickening series of pops, forcing him onto all fours. The shape of him changed rapidly now—hips lifting higher, torso lengthening, neck thrusting forward while his jaw pushed outward inch by inch.

His face—

God.

His mouth stretched too wide, teeth pressing down and lengthening until they spilled past his lips. The nose flattened and pulled forward, bones grinding as the skull reshaped itself into a long muzzle.

Through it all his eyes stayed the same.

Human. Wide. Trapped.

For one terrible second he looked straight at me, as if begging me to see him.

Then the last of the change ripped through him.

His chest expanded with a deep, shuddering breath, ribs flaring outward beneath a thick coat of fur. When he stood again he was taller than any man should be, shoulders massive, claws sinking into the earth with quiet strength.

The forest went completely still.

The creature lifted its head and sniffed the air.

Slowly, deliberately, those yellow eyes turned back to me.

And I realized the footsteps I’d heard before hadn’t been following me.

They’d been herding me.

:::writing
The rain had stopped, but the roof still dripped.

Water tapped through the broken skylight and pattered onto the concrete floor, each drop loud in the quiet. No one spoke. No one wanted to be the first.

Jonah lay propped against a stack of old paint buckets. His sleeve had been torn away hours ago. The bite sat on his forearm like a terrible punctuation mark—two dark crescents, swollen and angry, the skin around them already going gray.

Everyone kept glancing at it.

Jonah noticed. He gave a weak half‑smile.

“Seen worse,” he muttered.

No one laughed.

Mara paced in a tight line near the doorway, boots crunching glass. “We don’t know how long it takes,” she said for the fourth time. “Could be a day. Could be two.”

“Could be twenty minutes,” Eli replied quietly.

That hung in the air.

Across the room, Lila knelt beside Jonah. Her hands shook as she wrapped a clean strip of cloth around the bite, though they all knew it didn’t matter. Jonah watched her carefully, like he was memorizing her face.

“You’re doing it too tight,” he said gently.

“I know,” she whispered.

Her voice cracked on the last word.

Mara stopped pacing. “We have to decide.”

No one moved.

Outside, wind pushed against the broken windows, making the loose metal shutters rattle like bones.

Jonah cleared his throat. “Hey.”

They looked at him.

“I’ve seen what happens,” he said. “You all have.”

Images flickered through the room without anyone speaking them—the screaming, the teeth, the moment when someone’s eyes stopped belonging to them.

“I don’t want that,” Jonah said.

Lila shook her head immediately. “No. No, we wait.”

“Lil—”

“We wait.” Her voice rose, desperate. “Maybe it’s different. Maybe—”

“It’s not,” Eli said softly.

She turned on him like she might hit him.

But she didn’t.

Jonah shifted, wincing. The movement made a faint wet sound beneath the bandage. He stared at his arm for a moment, as if it belonged to someone else.

Then he looked back at them.

“You remember Sam?” he asked.

Everyone did.

They had waited too long with Sam.

Jonah exhaled slowly. “I won’t do that to you.”

Silence again. Heavy. Suffocating.

Finally Mara stepped forward. Her hand hovered near the pistol at her belt but didn’t touch it.

“I’ll do it,” she said.

Jonah shook his head.

“No,” he said. “Not you.”

His eyes moved across the room and stopped on Eli.

Eli froze.

“You’re steady,” Jonah said. “Always were.”

Eli’s face tightened like the words physically hurt.

“I can’t—”

“You can.”

Lila grabbed Jonah’s shirt. “Stop talking like it’s decided!”

Jonah took her hands. His were already cold.

“Hey,” he said softly.

She was crying openly now.

“I’m scared,” she said.

“I know.”

“I don’t want you to go.”

He swallowed. For a moment it looked like he might break too.

But instead he leaned forward and pressed his forehead to hers.

“Better me,” he whispered.

The rainwater dripped again through the skylight.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

Jonah leaned back and closed his eyes.

“Do it before I get sick,” he said.

Eli’s hands trembled as he drew the pistol. The metal looked enormous in the quiet room.

Mara turned away.

Lila clutched Jonah’s sleeve with both hands like she could anchor him to the world.

Jonah opened his eyes one last time.

“Hey,” he said, voice barely above a breath.

“Thanks for not leaving me out there.”

Eli’s jaw tightened.

The pistol lifted.

For a long moment, nobody breathed.

Then—

A single shot cracked through the empty building.

And after it, only the dripping roof remained.
:::

The silence after the act is enormous. The kind of silence that fills the lungs. No more arguments. No more watching the door, waiting for them to come back and say that one sentence again. The first thing he noticed was the sound.

A soft ticking. Slow. Patient. Like something that had already decided how the story would end.

When he opened his eyes, the ceiling above him was concrete, sweating with damp. A single lightbulb buzzed and swung gently, making the shadows tilt back and forth across the room. His head throbbed. Something cold circled his ankle.

He sat up too fast. The chain snapped tight with a metallic crack.

Memory came in fragments: a parking garage, footsteps behind him, the sour smell of chemicals. Then nothing.

The room was small. Bare. A rusted table stood a few feet away, just beyond the chain’s reach. On it sat a device—simple, deliberate. Metal. Heavy. Waiting.

And beside it, a tape recorder.

He stared at it for a long time before touching it. His fingers trembled as if the machine itself might bite.

The tape clicked.

A voice began to speak.

Calm. Measured. Almost polite.

By the time the message ended, the room felt smaller than before. The ticking was louder now, or maybe he had only started hearing it.

His eyes drifted back to the table.

The device wasn’t complicated. That was the worst part. It didn’t look like torture. It looked like a tool. Something ordinary that had been given a terrible purpose.

He understood immediately what it required.

His stomach folded in on itself.

“No,” he whispered to no one.

The chain scraped as he shifted back against the wall, as if distance could erase the choice waiting a few feet away. His mind began the frantic work of searching for loopholes—hidden doors, tricks, some detail the voice had lied about.

He tugged the chain again. Useless.

The ticking continued.

His gaze returned, again and again, to the table. To the shape of the thing waiting there. To the quiet promise it held: pain now, or something worse later.

He imagined the moment. The pressure. The sound it might make. His hands began to sweat.

A strange thought crept in, unwelcome and clear: people survived worse.

Immediately another voice answered: not by choice.

He laughed once, weakly, the sound cracking in the empty room.

“I can’t,” he said.

But his eyes had already begun measuring the distance.

Slowly, like approaching a wild animal, he crawled forward until the chain pulled taut again. His fingers stretched toward the table, barely brushing the metal edge. Cold. Real.

His breathing grew shallow.

Up close, the tool looked heavier than he expected. Final.

His hands hovered above it, trembling so badly he had to pull them back and wipe them against his shirt. The ticking seemed to echo inside his chest now, each second pushing him closer to the same impossible edge.

He tried to imagine walking out of the room afterward. Fresh air. Sky. The absurd normalcy of it.

Then he looked at his own hands.

They didn’t look like the hands of someone who could do what the voice demanded.

But the timer kept ticking.

After a long while, he reached for the tool again.

This time he didn’t pull his hand away.

Upstairs, something shifted.

Jamie froze.

“Dad?” A little louder now. “You home?”

No answer.

From the living room doorway, a tall shape watched.

It had been standing there long before Jamie arrived, pressed into the corner where the hallway light never quite reached. Still as furniture. Breathing slowly through its nose.

The blade in the intruder’s hand caught the faintest sliver of light from the streetlamp outside. A thin silver line. Then darkness again as the hand lowered.

Jamie took a few cautious steps toward the kitchen.

Another creak.

Jamie turned their head sharply toward the stairs.

The intruder moved.

Just one silent step forward. Close enough now to see the back of Jamie’s jacket. Close enough to hear the uneven breathing.

Jamie rubbed their arms.

“Why is it so cold in here…?”

Behind them, the knife lifted slightly.

And the house remained perfectly, carefully quiet.

The office was quiet except for the slow tick of the wall clock.

Marino stood by the window, hands folded behind his back, watching the rain smear the city lights. Across the desk, Luca shifted in his chair but didn’t speak.

“Funny thing about trust,” Marino said softly. “You build it brick by brick. Years sometimes.” He turned, his expression calm. “Then one day somebody decides the house looks better without a foundation.”

Luca nodded once. “About Carlo…”

“Yes. Carlo.” Marino walked back to his chair and sat, smoothing his cuffs. “I hear he’s been… talking. To people who don’t deserve the conversation.”

“That’s what we hear.”

Marino sighed, like a disappointed teacher. “Carlo’s been with us a long time. Ate at my table. Held my kids when they were babies.” A pause. “Which makes this… unfortunate.”

Luca waited.

Marino picked up a small silver lighter, turning it in his fingers. “A man who forgets where his bread is buttered sometimes needs a change of scenery.”

“You want him sent away.”

“Far away.” Marino’s eyes lifted. Cold. Final. “Someplace quiet. No phones. No more conversations.”

Luca understood. “Tonight?”

Marino flicked the lighter open, then shut. Click.

“Tonight,” he said. “Before Carlo has the chance to pack a suitcase.”

“And the others?”

“They’ll hear he took a long walk and didn’t come back.” Marino shrugged lightly. “The city’s full of dark corners.”

Luca stood.

At the door he paused. “Anything you want me to tell him?”

Marino leaned back in his chair.

“Tell him,” he said, “the family thanks him for his years of service.”

Another click of the lighter.

“And wish him a peaceful retirement.”

By the time the parking lot emptied, Mira was the only one left.

The wind slid between the rows of cars, carrying the distant hiss of the highway. She stood beside Daniel Rourke’s sedan and watched the yellow security light flicker against its polished hood. Her hands were steady now. That surprised her.

Three months ago they had trembled in a hospital corridor while a doctor explained words that sounded like broken glass: spinal damage, permanent, unlikely to walk again.

Her brother had been driving home from work when Rourke’s company truck ran the light.

Not an accident, the police had said. Negligence. Faulty maintenance. Cut corners.

But the fines had been paid. The lawyers had smiled their thin, practiced smiles. Rourke himself had stood outside the courthouse telling reporters it was “an unfortunate situation.”

Unfortunate.

Mira looked at the quiet car in front of her.

She told herself this wasn’t revenge. Not really. It was balance. Correction. The world had tilted when her brother’s life split in half on a rainy Tuesday night, and no one—not the courts, not the company, not the man who signed the safety reports—had bothered to tilt it back.

Someone had to.

She pictured her brother’s wheelchair beside the kitchen window. The way he joked about it, as if humor could sand down the edges of the truth. The way he stopped going out with friends. The silence that filled their parents’ house now.

Rourke still drove home every night. Still played golf on weekends. Still posted photos of smiling vacations.

The world had decided that was acceptable.

Mira knelt beside the car.

If something happened on the road tomorrow, people would call it tragic. A mechanical failure. One of those things. The same language they had used before.

Unfortunate.

Her chest tightened, not with fear but with a strange, cold clarity. She told herself that a man who gambled with other people’s lives had already chosen the rules. She was only playing the game he started.

Still, another voice whispered: This is killing.

Mira closed her eyes.

Maybe. Maybe not. Cars failed every day. People lived, people died, and no jury ever untangled every cause. The universe was messy like that.

And what was one more accident in a world already full of them?

She stood, hands cold in the wind, and looked once more at the empty lot.

“Balance,” she said softly, as if the word itself could make it true.
:::

The dog was all ribs and teeth, its coat clotted with dust and old scars. It growled low over the scrap in the dirt—a strip of something that might once have been meat, stiff and gray. The sound it made wasn’t just warning. It was the sound of the same hunger clawing through both of them.

The man’s hands shook as he stepped closer. His stomach felt like a hollow furnace, burning and empty at once. Three days since the last real meal. Two since even a mouthful of anything. The smell of the scrap—rot and salt—hit him like a promise.

The dog lunged first.

They collided in the dirt, a tangle of limbs and snapping jaws. He caught the animal by the scruff with one hand, the other shoving hard against its neck as its teeth snapped inches from his face. Its body was wiry with desperation, stronger than its starved frame should have allowed. Claws raked his arms. He grunted, forcing it down, but it twisted and thrashed, fighting with the blind fury of something that knew losing meant dying.

For a moment they froze, faces close, breath hot and ragged. Two starving creatures, each smelling the other’s weakness.

Then the dog went for his throat.

He slammed it aside, fingers digging in, pushing, choking, wrestling it into the dirt. The growls turned to harsh, choking barks. His vision tunneled with hunger and fear and a dull, pounding rage. He didn’t think about the dog anymore—only the scrap.

When the animal finally broke away and fled limping into the ruins, the man collapsed beside the food. His hands were shaking so badly he could barely lift it.

He didn’t check what it was.

He just ate.

The warehouse looks smaller at night.

In the day it’s just another dead building—corrugated walls, busted windows, weeds forcing their way through the cracked loading dock. But in the dark it feels like a witness. Like it knows.

He stands beside the rusted side door, lighter in one hand, the other shoved deep in his jacket pocket. The air smells like dust and old oil. One spark, he tells himself. That’s all it would take to turn the silence into something roaring.

The thought sends a quick, electric pulse through him—half excitement, half nausea.

He flicks the lighter once. A small flame rises, steady and yellow. It wavers in the breeze, fragile, almost harmless. Hard to believe something that small could eat a building.

He imagines it spreading—first along the dusty floor, then climbing beams, licking up the walls. Sirens in the distance. The sky turning orange.

For a second the image feels like power.

Then it feels like a line he can’t uncross.

The lighter snaps shut. The darkness returns, thicker than before. He stares at the door, breathing slowly, as if the building itself is waiting to see what kind of man he’s going to be.

“That's not the amount we agreed on,” Lenny said, staring into the open duffel.

“It’s the amount you’re getting,” Marco replied. His voice had the tight edge of someone who hadn’t slept and couldn’t afford to lose.

For a moment neither moved. Somewhere down the block a siren wailed and faded.

Lenny’s hand dipped into his jacket.

Marco saw the motion a half second too late. The knife flashed out, dull steel catching the sickly light. Instinct took over. Marco lunged, grabbing Lenny’s wrist before the blade could swing free. “Let go,” Lenny hissed.

“Drop it!”

The blade jerked between them like a compass needle gone wild. Marco felt it skid across his jacket, then slip underneath.

The sensation came a beat later.

At first it was just pressure, like someone had punched him hard in the ribs. Then heat spread outward from the spot, sharp and electric. His breath vanished from his lungs. When he tried to inhale, the air came in shallow, trembling pulls, and the burning line in his side flared brighter.

Marco staggered back, one hand clamping over the wound. The warmth seeping through his fingers made his stomach drop.

Across from him, Lenny held the knife out, chest heaving, eyes wide now—not angry anymore.

Just scared.

Neither of them had planned for it to go this far.
:::

:::writing
The alley smelled like wet cardboard and old blood.

Detective Mara Ionescu paused beneath the sagging fire escape and let the rain bead on the brim of her hat. A police cruiser idled at the mouth of the alley, red and blue light smearing across brick and puddles. The uniforms had done their best to keep the scene clean, but the place still had that metallic tang that clung to the back of the throat.

She slipped on gloves.

The body lay half on its side beside an overturned trash bin, one arm crooked under the torso as if the man had tried to push himself up and changed his mind halfway through. His coat was dark enough that the spreading stain across the ribs almost blended in, but the rain kept worrying at it, thinning it into rusty threads that ran toward the gutter.

Mara crouched.

The alley was narrow enough that the walls held the smell in—rot, grease from the diner vent two doors down, and the sharp copper scent rising from the body. Somewhere above, a window rattled in the wind. Water dripped steadily from a bent gutter and tapped the pavement beside the dead man’s ear.

Tap. Tap. Tap.

She pulled the coat back just enough to see the work.

Knife, most likely. Several entries, tight grouping under the left side. Whoever did it hadn’t been wild about it. Quick. Close. Personal. The fabric was cut clean where the blade had gone in and out, the edges dark and stiff.

“Wallet?” she asked.

A uniform behind her flipped open an evidence bag. “Empty. No ID.”

Of course.

Mara studied the man’s hands. Dirt under the nails. A split knuckle on the right. Recent. He’d fought, at least for a second or two. The rain had washed the pavement clean except for a faint smear near the wall where his heel must’ve slid.

She leaned closer. The body was already cooling; the damp air accelerated that. The skin had that dull, waxy look that came when heat left faster than it should.

Her gaze moved slowly, methodically—collar, jawline, pockets, the ground around him.

People always expected something dramatic in moments like this. Shock. Anger. Revulsion.

But murder scenes were puzzles, not tragedies. The tragedy had already happened.

Mara stood, pulling off one glove with her teeth.

“Who found him?”

“Garbage pickup,” the uniform said. “Driver came through the alley early.”

She looked once more at the man on the pavement, rain dimpling the shallow pools around his body.

“Yeah,” she said quietly. “That figures.”
:::

Caleb Rook liked it that way.

He dusted them every morning with a soft brush, murmuring apologies when the bristles snagged a sleeve or collar. “Still as statues,” he would say proudly, stepping back to admire the room. “Perfect.”

He had once been a taxidermist by trade—foxes, deer, the occasional hawk brought in by farmers who wanted their trophies preserved. But animals bored him. They were predictable. They did not have stories in their eyes.

A fisherman with engine trouble.

When the work was done, he dressed them in clean clothes and carried them upstairs.

Another figure for the collection.

Another story frozen perfectly in place.

Visitors sometimes said the room felt crowded. As if the figures were watching.

Caleb would smile at that.

“Of course they are,” he’d reply softly, straightening a collar or adjusting a hand.

“They’re guests.”

The patrol officers had already taken the parents to the station. Neighbors whispered on lawns. Animal control had carried a small covered box out the front door.

Now it was just the detective and the child’s room.

He nudged the door open with two fingers.

The room looked ordinary in the way that made his stomach tighten: glow‑in‑the‑dark stars on the ceiling, a pile of stuffed animals, a neatly made bed with cartoon rockets on the blanket. On the desk sat a school notebook, open to a page torn halfway out.

Something had been written carefully in pencil.

Alvarez stepped closer.

The handwriting was round and patient, the way teachers liked—each letter deliberate, almost proud of itself.

At the top of the page it said:

“I’m not bad.”

Below it:

“I tried to explain but nobody listens when you’re little. They say I’m imagining things.”

The detective pulled on gloves and lifted the paper.

More lines followed.

“I loved Daisy. I really did. She slept on my bed every night and licked my fingers when I cried. That’s why it had to be me.”

The pencil marks pressed harder into the paper now.

“She started looking at me different yesterday. Not like a dog. Like she knew something. Like she could see the thoughts I was having.”

A long pause in the writing. Then:

“I tried telling Mom that Daisy wasn’t Daisy anymore. Mom said I was being silly.”

“I waited a long time to make sure.”

“I watched her breathing while she slept.”

“I said sorry first.”

The last lines were smaller, squeezed near the bottom edge of the page.

“You have to stop things before they become problems. That’s what adults always say.”

“So I did.”

Then, almost as an afterthought:

“I hope Daisy understands.”

Alvarez lowered the page slowly.

From the hallway behind him, an officer called, “Detective? You need to see this.”

Alvarez folded the note once.

On the back of the page, in the same careful handwriting, was one more sentence.

“I’m glad it worked.”

He stared at it a long moment before asking, quietly:

“Where’s the kid now?”

A dry, restless feeling under Mara’s skin, as if something beneath it wanted air. She scratched absentmindedly during the day, harder at night, until faint curls of skin began to lift along her forearms like peeling paint. When she pulled one loose, it came away too easily—thin, pale, and wrong. Underneath, the new skin looked darker, thicker. Tough.

Her joints started next.

One evening she reached for a glass and felt her fingers lock. A pressure built deep in her hand, followed by a dull, internal crack. Not sharp pain—worse. A slow rearranging. Her bones seemed to soften, bend, then settle again in a shape her hand had never held before. The glass shattered in her grip.

After that, the changes came faster.

Her shoulders crept wider each morning. Her spine arched, vertebrae shifting with quiet pops when she moved. Sometimes, in the dark, her ribs would flex inward as if something inside her chest were testing the cage.

She stopped calling friends. Their voices began to sound strange to her—thin, fragile. Like prey animals making polite noises.

Morality didn’t vanish all at once. It slipped away in small permissions.

At first she told herself the stray cat had probably been sick anyway. Then she told herself the neighbor shouldn’t have wandered into the woods at night. Later still, she stopped explaining things at all.

But the worst change wasn’t the body.

It was the quiet, growing certainty that nothing about this felt wrong anymore.

Not the soft dark of a closed room. This is thick, pressing dark, like the inside of a fist.

thud.

A dull weight lands on the lid above their face.

Thud.  
Scrape.  
Thud.

Dirt.

Their chest tightens. They try to shout but the sound rebounds off the wood and slams back into their ears, small and useless. The air already feels wrong—too warm, too breathed.

They press their palms upward. The lid doesn’t move.

More dirt falls. Faster now.

Thudthudthud.

Each impact sends a faint shower of dust through the seams, the smell of earth trickling down into the coffin. The sound above grows muffled as the soil piles higher, the world sealing shut one shovelful at a time.

Their breaths shorten.

In. Hot.

Out. Hotter.

The coffin seems to shrink with every inhale.

And above them, the dirt keeps falling.

By the time Mara Ellison noticed the pattern, she had already begun to look forward to Mondays.

Mondays were when the photographs arrived.

They came in sterile digital folders from field teams: living rooms dusted with powder, alleyways taped in yellow, bedrooms frozen mid-breath. Most investigators opened them like chores. Mara opened them like galleries.

She would dim the lights in her office and let the monitor glow against the metal cabinets. The first rule of forensics was detachment. Evidence, not emotion. Measurements, not stories.

But scenes had compositions. Anyone could see that.

The spill of a broken wine bottle across tile. The geometry of blood droplets radiating from a single point like a dark constellation. A chair tipped just slightly off-balance, as if still remembering motion.

People called it violence.

Mara sometimes thought of it as arrangement.

The Riverside case arrived late one evening.

A patrol officer had found the body in a greenhouse behind an abandoned house. The folder contained forty-seven photographs. Mara opened the first and felt something unfamiliar—almost a shiver of anticipation.

The greenhouse roof had shattered in places, letting winter light fall through jagged panes. Dust and pollen hung in the air like gold powder. In the center of the room, among long-dead vines, lay the victim.

But it wasn't the body that caught her breath.

It was the way everything aligned.

The victim lay on their back atop a collapsed wooden table, arms loosely outspread, as if placed rather than dropped. Above them, the broken glass created a fractured halo of light. Thin vines had draped themselves over the limbs, curling gently around wrists and shoulders like deliberate decoration.

And the blood—

Not sprayed, not chaotic.

A narrow line had run from beneath the torso and followed the grooves in the greenhouse floor, branching outward through cracks in the concrete. In the photos it resembled ink spreading through paper fibers, delicate and organic.

Mara leaned closer to the screen.

Someone had moved the flowerpots.

She could tell by the rings of clean concrete beneath them. Six pots now formed a loose circle around the body. Inside each, brittle stems leaned inward as if bowing.

The light shifted between photos as the crime-scene techs moved. Each angle changed the balance of the scene: shadow crossing the face, vines forming soft diagonals, glass glittering like frost above it all.

It looked less like a murder.

More like an installation.

Mara zoomed into one image.

The victim’s hand rested palm-up. In the palm sat a single white camellia. Fresh. Untouched by the surrounding decay.

She felt an odd sensation then—something between professional curiosity and quiet admiration.

Whoever had done this had stayed long enough to see the room the way she saw it.

Most killers fled chaos.

This one had composed it.

For the first time in years, Mara printed the photographs instead of leaving them on the screen. She laid them across her desk, adjusting their positions, studying the lines that connected one frame to the next.

Evidence, she reminded herself.

Still, her eyes kept drifting back to the greenhouse wide shot.

The light.

The symmetry.

The careful placement of the flower.

And beneath the clinical part of her mind that cataloged angles, timelines, and fibers, another thought slowly rooted itself:

Someone out there understood the same terrible beauty she did.
:::

“Hello?” he tried, and immediately wished he hadn’t.

Something raked across his back. No shape, no warning—just a sudden tearing pressure that shoved the breath out of him. His body lurched forward and he crashed to his knees. For a second he couldn’t even understand what had happened. Then the heat bloomed across his shoulders, sharp and wet.

He twisted around.

Nothing.

Just trees. Dark trunks. Empty air.

A second hit landed across his ribs, a blunt impact followed by a slicing burn that felt like hot wire dragged through skin. He cried out and staggered sideways, clutching at himself. His fingers came away slick.

“Stop—!” he gasped, spinning in place.

The worst part wasn’t the pain.

It was the waiting.

Every nerve strained for a clue: a shifting shadow, a breath on his neck, a bend in the grass. But the night held perfectly still, as if the forest itself refused to show him what hunted him.

Something brushed his ankle.

He jumped back with a scream, but the ground behind him vanished and he fell hard against a rock. The impact jarred through his spine. For a moment he lay there, shaking, staring into the black space above him.

Slow this time.

He stared into the darkness, eyes wide, tears cutting warm lines across cold skin.

The thing above him waited a moment longer.

Then the air beside his ear trembled, as if something enormous had leaned closer to listen.

:::writing
They made him stand between them.

A single lantern swung from a beam above, its light moving slowly across the room like a lazy pendulum. Every pass lit one face, then the other.

Jonas to the left. Mira to the right.

Both bound. Both bruised. Both trying, very hard, not to look afraid.

The commander placed a revolver on the table in front of him. The metal clicked softly against the wood.

“Choose,” the man said.

The word was casual, almost bored.

His legs refused to move. His mind tried to reject the shape of the moment, like a tongue probing a broken tooth that couldn’t possibly be real.

“Don’t,” Mira said quietly. “Don’t play their game.”

Jonas laughed once under his breath. “He doesn’t have a choice.”

The lantern swung again. Light passed over Jonas’s face—tired, steady. They had shared a room for two years during the winter campaign. Cards, bad jokes, long arguments about nothing.

Then darkness.

Then Mira in the light. The person who had dragged him out of a collapsed building with a dislocated shoulder and a scream he still heard in dreams.

His chest tightened until breathing hurt.

“I can’t,” he said.

The commander shrugged. “Then we shoot both.”

One of the soldiers lifted his rifle slightly to demonstrate.

The room felt suddenly smaller, like the walls had moved in an inch.

Jonas looked at him. “Hey.”

The simple word broke something inside him.

Jonas shook his head faintly. “You know which one of us is more useful to them.”

Mira snapped, “Shut up.”

“You’re a medic,” Jonas said gently. “You save people.”

“I’m not saving anyone like this.”

The lantern creaked. Back and forth. Back and forth.

The commander tapped the revolver.

“Choose.”

His thoughts shattered into fragments. Memories. Laughter. A night by a river. Mira stitching his arm while cursing at him. Jonas stealing the last piece of bread.

His body started shaking.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered, though he didn’t know to whom.

“Don’t you dare,” Mira said, sudden fire in her voice.

Jonas just watched him.

And nodded.

The smallest nod. Permission. Forgiveness. A final kindness he didn’t deserve.

His hand lifted.

His finger pointed.

For a moment no one moved.

Then the commander smiled thinly and gestured.

The gunshot cracked through the room.

The lantern swung violently from the shock of it.

When the light came back across the floor, there was a dark spread beneath the chair and one less voice in the world.

He didn’t remember falling, but suddenly he was on his knees.

Somewhere behind him the commander said, almost pleasantly, “See? That wasn’t so hard.”

But the echo of the shot kept repeating in his skull, again and again, long after the lantern finally stopped swinging.
:::

The hotel room smelled faintly of solvent and cheap citrus cleaner. City lights blinked through the half‑closed curtains.

Mara sat cross‑legged on the bed with a disassembled pistol spread across a white towel. She hummed off‑key while running a cloth along the barrel.

Across the room, Leon leaned back in a chair, balancing a long case across his knees while he polished a metal component with patient, circular motions.

“You know,” Mara said, squinting through the barrel toward the lamp, “I still think quiet is best.”

Leon snorted. “Quiet is boring.”

“Boring keeps you alive.”

“Distance keeps you alive.” He held the piece up to the light like a jeweler inspecting a diamond. “Clean. Efficient. You’re already halfway down the street before anyone knows something happened.”

Mara clicked her tongue. “Too impersonal. Might as well send a letter.”

“That’s the point.”

She reassembled the pistol with a soft series of clicks and rested it on the towel. “I like to know the job is finished.”

Leon glanced over. “You worry too much.”

“And you trust physics too much.”

He shrugged. “Physics has never betrayed me.”

Mara leaned back on her hands. “You ever notice how people always imagine this work as dramatic? Screaming, chaos, all that.”

“Movies.”

“Yeah. In reality it’s mostly… maintenance.” She nudged the gun oil bottle with a finger. “Cleaning. Waiting. Bad hotel art.”

Leon followed her gaze to the crooked painting of a sailboat above the dresser.

“Terrible sailboat,” he said.

“The worst.”

A moment passed.

Leon closed the case with a quiet snap. “Still,” he added, standing, “distance.”

Mara slid the pistol into its case and zipped it shut.

“Quiet,” she replied.

They both paused.

“Teamwork?” Leon suggested.

Mara smiled faintly. “Teamwork.”

The necromancer worked in a field that had once been a battlefield and was now something worse.

Graves had not been dug here; the earth had merely tried and failed to swallow what war had left behind. Helmets rusted half-buried. Fingers jutted from the soil like pale roots. The air carried the sweet, sour stink of rot thick enough to taste.

He raised his staff.

The magic did not feel like fire or lightning or any honest force of nature. It was colder. Thicker. As if the night itself had curdled and begun to move.

The ground trembled.

A hand pushed through the soil—skin split and gray, nails black with packed dirt. Then another. Bodies followed, dragging themselves upward with stiff, uncertain movements. Armor hung loosely over collapsed ribcages. Faces sagged where flesh had softened and slipped from bone. One corpse turned its head too far, vertebrae clicking softly, yet it did not stop moving.

The necromancer spoke a final word.

Something answered.

Not from the sky, not from the earth—but from the corpses themselves. A quiet obedience settled into them, wrong as a heartbeat in a stone. Empty sockets turned toward him. Jaws opened with wet creaks.

They stood.

Not alive. Not truly dead.

And the field, which had once held silence, now waited for war again.

The alley smelled like wet concrete and old smoke. Six of them stood in a loose half-circle, their shadows long under the flickering streetlight. No one spoke at first. They just watched him.

“Look at me,” the leader said.

Rico was older than the rest, calm in a way that made the others quiet when he breathed in. The recruit forced his eyes up.

“You said you wanted in,” Rico continued. “Said you were ready to be family.”

The others murmured. Someone chuckled under their breath.

Rico gestured toward the man on his knees a few feet away, wrists tied, head bowed. “Family means we trust you. And trust means you do what needs doing.”

The recruit’s hands shook. He tried to hide it, curling his fingers into fists.

One of the gang members stepped closer behind him and whispered, almost friendly, “Everyone here did it. Every one of us. That’s how you know nobody walks away.”

Rico held out a weapon.

The metal looked heavier than it should have.

“Take it,” Rico said.

The recruit hesitated.

The circle tightened. Someone nudged his shoulder. Another voice from the dark said, “Don’t freeze now. You been talking big all week.”

Rico’s voice hardened. “You walk away tonight, you walk away alone. And you better hope we never see you again.”

The recruit swallowed and took the weapon.

For a moment everything went silent except the buzzing streetlight.

“Do it,” Rico said.

The recruit stepped forward. The man on the ground didn’t look up.

Behind him the gang waited, unmoving, like judges who had already decided the verdict. The recruit felt every eye on his back, every expectation pressing down.

His grip tightened.

When it was over, the alley was quiet again.

Rico stepped forward, resting a hand on the recruit’s shoulder. “Now,” he said, calm again, “you’re one of us.”

:::writing
He salts everything before he tastes it. I had forgotten that.

A small white rain over the potatoes, over the green beans, over the roast. My roast. I watch his hand shake the shaker with the lazy confidence of a man who believes the evening is ordinary.

“Smells incredible,” he says.

“Thank you,” I tell him, and sip my wine so I don’t smile too widely.

The dining room is warm. Candles, soft light, the window cracked open just enough for the night air. I made it comfortable. I wanted him relaxed, unguarded. I wanted him to eat slowly.

He cuts into the meat. Steam rises. The first bite disappears between casual conversation about work, about traffic, about a neighbor’s dog that won’t stop barking.

Nothing yet.

Of course nothing yet.

He chews, swallows, wipes the corner of his mouth with the napkin. My heart beats harder than I expected. I had imagined feeling calm. Clinical. Instead I feel like a gambler watching the wheel spin.

He takes another bite.

“So,” he says, pointing his fork at me, “you never told me why you suddenly wanted dinner tonight.”

“I missed you,” I say.

That makes him laugh.

The third bite is when he pauses.

It’s small. Almost nothing. Just a slight hesitation while reaching for his glass of water. His brow creases like he’s forgotten a word.

“You alright?” I ask, gentle.

“Yeah,” he says. “Just… weird taste.”

He drinks.

The poison has no taste, of course. That part was important.

We talk about the weather for another minute before he loosens his collar.

“Hot in here?” he asks.

“Is it?”

He nods slowly, though the window is open and I feel almost cold. A faint flush climbs his neck. He presses his tongue to the inside of his cheek like he’s bitten it.

I watch his throat.

Swallow.

Swallow again.

Now he shifts in his chair. The first real discomfort. His hand drifts to his stomach, not dramatically, just resting there like he’s suddenly aware of it.

“You didn’t—” He stops.

“Didn’t what?”

“Nothing. I just feel… strange.”

He laughs again, but it’s thinner this time.

I tilt my head, concerned. Practiced concern.

“Maybe you ate too fast.”

“Maybe.”

He reaches for another bite, stubbornly normal. I admire that. Truly. The body, though, has started its quiet rebellion. His fingers don’t close around the fork quite right. It clinks softly against the plate.

The conversation stumbles.

“How’s your sister?” he asks.

“Good,” I say.

“Good… good…”

He loses the thread. His eyes drift downward, unfocused for a moment. When he looks back up, there’s confusion there now. Real confusion.

“What’s in this?” he asks.

“Rosemary,” I say. “Garlic. Butter.”

He nods as if processing takes effort.

The sweating starts next. Small beads along his hairline. He wipes them with the back of his hand and chuckles nervously.

“I think something’s wrong.”

I reach across the table and place my hand over his.

It’s already colder than it should be.

“You’re okay,” I say softly.

But he’s breathing deeper now. His chest lifts harder with each inhale. His chair scrapes slightly as he shifts again, trying to find a comfortable position inside a body that is becoming unfamiliar.

“What did you—”

The sentence collapses halfway through. His fingers tighten around mine with sudden strength.

And there it is.

The moment realization arrives.

His eyes search my face the way people look at locked doors.

I hold his gaze. Calm. Patient. The way you sit with someone through a difficult meal.

“You should have tasted it before salting,” I tell him quietly.

He tries to stand, but the signal between mind and muscle has begun to fray. The chair tips. The candles flicker in the sudden movement.

The room grows very quiet except for his breathing.

I remain seated, watching, as the dinner finally settles.
:::

:::writing
The plank bowed slightly under his weight.

Below it, the sea moved like a dark, breathing thing. Fins cut the surface in slow, patient circles.

“Captain… please.” The mutineer’s voice shook so badly the words almost fell apart. Salt wind whipped his hair across his eyes. “I only spoke what the others were thinking.”

Behind him, the pirates watched in a crooked line along the rail. No one spoke. A few wouldn’t even look.

Captain Varrick rested one boot on the start of the plank, arms folded. His face held the calm patience of a man watching the tide.

“You spoke,” he said quietly, “about putting a knife in my back.”

The mutineer’s bare feet edged forward another inch. The plank creaked. Beneath him, a shark’s dorsal fin sliced past the hull, followed by another… and another. The water churned with shadows.

“I was angry,” the man whispered. “I didn’t mean—”

“Last step.”

The mutineer stared down at the sea. The sharks had begun to gather directly below the plank now, pale bellies flashing as they rolled through the water. One of them bumped the hull with a hollow thud.

His breath came in sharp, broken gasps.

“I don’t want to die.”

Captain Varrick shrugged. “Should’ve thought of that before the mutiny.”

For a long moment the man stood frozen at the end of the plank, toes hanging over empty air. The ship creaked. The sharks circled faster.

Then his foot slipped.

He vanished with a splash.

For half a heartbeat there was only rippling water.

Then the sea exploded.

Fins thrashed. White water churned as the sharks surged together in a violent frenzy, colliding and twisting over one another. The surface frothed and rolled as if the ocean itself were boiling.

The crew watched in silence.

Within seconds, the water stilled again. The fins drifted apart, circling lazily once more.

Captain Varrick turned away from the rail.

“Let that be a lesson,” he said. “My ship sails one way.”
:::

:::writing
He first heard the footsteps three nights after the murder.

Soft. Bare. Following him from room to room.

At first he blamed the house. Old wood settles, pipes sigh, wind nudges doors that never quite latch. Reasonable things. Explainable things.

But the steps matched his.

When he stopped walking, they stopped too.

He told himself not to look behind him.

The fourth night, the smell came. Damp earth and iron. It seeped through the hallway like fog, thick enough to taste. He scrubbed the floors though they were already clean. He washed his hands until the skin split.

Still the smell clung to him.

Still the footsteps followed.

By the sixth night he started seeing her.

Not clearly. Never fully. Just pieces.

A pale hand resting on the kitchen table that vanished when he blinked. A shape sitting in the corner chair that melted back into shadow when he turned his head. Once, in the bathroom mirror, he saw her standing behind him with her head tilted in that same quiet way she had right before he struck.

He shattered the mirror with his fist.

But the worst was the whispering.

It came from everywhere. The vents. The ceiling. Inside the walls.

At first it sounded like wind squeezing through cracks.

Then it started to form words.

"You remember."

He pressed pillows over his ears.

"You remember."

He began leaving every light on in the house. Lamps, kitchen lights, even the oven light. But the brightness only made the shadows sharper, darker, deeper.

And she lived in the shadows.

On the ninth night he finally saw her clearly.

She stood at the end of the hallway.

Not bloody. Not rotting. Just wrong. Her neck bent slightly where it should not bend. Her eyes wide and patient, as if she had all the time in the world.

He couldn't move.

Her wet footprints appeared one by one on the floor between them.

Step.

Step.

Step.

He squeezed his eyes shut and began to scream that he was sorry.

When he opened them again, she was inches from his face.

Her mouth slowly opened.

But the voice that came out was his own.

Over and over.

"I remember."
:::

The horn sounded across the dead city at dawn.

It echoed between the skeletons of towers and the hollow shells of malls where wind pushed dust through shattered glass. Somewhere in the distance, drones whirred like insects, their red lights sweeping the streets.

Mara ran.

Her lungs burned. The tracking band around her wrist pulsed every few seconds, broadcasting her location to anyone wealthy enough to be watching the Hunt today. Every step splashed through shallow rainwater and old ash. The rules were simple: run until sunset. If you were still alive, you were free.

No one ever was.

She heard the motorcycle before she saw it.

A low engine growl rolled through the streets, slow and confident. The kind of sound made by someone who knew the race was already over.

Mara ducked into a collapsed subway entrance, stumbling down cracked concrete stairs. Darkness swallowed her. She pressed herself against the wall, trying to quiet her breathing.

The engine cut off above.

Silence.

Then boots on the stairs.

Measured. Unhurried.

A flashlight beam slid down the tunnel and stopped on her wrist. The band blinked red.

“Well,” the hunter said, voice calm, almost friendly. “There you are.”

He stepped closer, rifle resting casually against his shoulder, visor reflecting her terrified face. His armor was polished, sponsor logos shining along the plates. A camera drone hovered behind him, recording.

Mara backed away until the cold tunnel wall stopped her.

“Please,” she whispered.

The hunter tilted his head slightly, studying her like an animal that had run well.

“Good distance today,” he said. “Crowd loves a runner with spirit.”

He raised the rifle.

The shot cracked through the empty subway.

For a moment, only the drone’s camera buzz remained.

The hunter lowered the weapon and walked forward, kneeling beside the still body. He unclipped the tracking band from Mara’s wrist and held it up to the hovering drone.

“Tag secured,” he said.

Above ground, somewhere far away in a glittering city that never saw the Hunts, millions of viewers cheered as the scoreboard updated.

RUNNER 47 — ELIMINATED.

The hunter stood, pocketed the band, and headed back toward the stairs.

“Next round starts in ten,” his earpiece crackled.

He smiled.
:::
